Hey i wanted to make sure that a few things are clear that im not so sure if you entirely captured in the document but it is worth doing soin, so there is no changes in the wrong directions.  how i see the seam mending between the two, is i like the approach i have, but the model for example needs help with being molded. thats where blockbench ideas are coming in, i dont want to make one big player model i want to, and as i already do, make each part, and then mend them together. same thing id like to do for cars. so that i can make a a bunch of tires for example, or spoilers, or whatever, and they just connect to the bodys that are made seperately, i had another claude get me a summary of the bones system because this is exactly the same idea i want for vehicles, or even props is: Animation & bones in hmsc-int — current state

  There are two cleanly separated modules, captured fresh on 2026-06-05 from the old head_lab
  code, and one hard architectural rule sitting on top of both.

  1. The skeleton (game/figure/) — bones and forward kinematics

  skeleton.ts is the heart. It defines a fixed 25-bone skeleton:

  - torso (root), head, pelvis
  - per side: Shoulder → UpperArm → Elbow → Forearm → Wrist → Hand
  - per side: Hip → Thigh → Knee → Shin → Foot

  buildSkeleton(shapeId, pose, phase, actions) is pure forward kinematics, hand-built in local
  space — torso is root, pelvis/head/shoulders hang off it, limbs chain joint→joint. Each bone
  is {position, rotation, scale, thickness, hitbox} where the hitbox is an oriented-box hit 
  volume (V2-ruled: these boxes are the game's hit volumes, no separate collision shapes).

  Bones (a Record<BoneId, SkeletonBone>) is described as the kit's "universal currency" —
  assembly, clothing, hitboxes, anchors, and the future ragdoll all speak it.

  Inputs that drive a pose:
  - pose — stand/walk/flex/wave etc. (BodyPoseId), gait driven by phase (a sin walk-cycle clock)
  - actions — RigTimelineAction[], the V6 action vocabulary.
  actionWeight/actionPhase/actionArg/actionOsc read these by family (arm/leg/head/torso/body…)
  and side, with both_/left_/right_ target matching. This is what layers crouch, punches
  (jab/cross/hook/uppercut/body), waves, sit/lay on top of the base pose.
  
  rig.ts assembles the full dressed figure for one moment. BodyRigFrame = bones + assembly + 
  anatomy + clothing + hitboxes + anchors. Two doors in, only two:
  - buildRigFrame(shape, pose, phase, actions, clothing…) — an authored pose
  - buildRigFrameFromBones(bones, …) — the physics seam: feed a custom bones record and the
  whole dressed figure follows (pose/phase never enter; the bones are the pose)
  
  It also rules 6 damage zones (head/torso/lArm/rArm/lLeg/rLeg) with a 25-bone→6-zone map, and
  semantic anchors (face, face_grab, eyes, mouth, neck, left/right_palm, grab origins) — where
  interactions like grab/punch/hold attach.

  2. The action layer (game/animation/) — the V6 animation DSL

  This is the one animation path (per-cart pose tables are retired). It's a parser + sampler,
  deliberately not tied to figures:

  - DSL format: bracket groups [...] = sequential steps; ; = parallel actions in a step; | =
  pipe fallback; fields are duration, target, action, args.... Example: [0.5, right arm, 
  lift-and-bend, fast; 1.25, l_fist, clench],[2, head_face, talk].
  - parseAnimationDsl(src) → AnimationTimeline (steps + total).
  - sampleAnimationTimeline(timeline, seconds) → SampledAction[] with phase + weight. The only 
  easing is sin(phase·π) — no other curves (no ruling exists for them).
  - Looping: any action ending _loop, or the exact name shake_in_air, loops the whole timeline;
  otherwise it clamps.
  - A big ANIMATION_TARGET_ALIASES table normalizes arm→both_arms, tire→wheels, car→vehicle,
  etc. — covers body, face, and vehicle targets.

  Exposed as the frozen GAME_ANIMATION object. Note the explicit boundary: this module never 
  reaches into game/figure/ — consumers translate SampledAction[] into bone actions themselves
  (the SampledAction shape is structurally the same as RigTimelineAction, so it casts straight
  through).

  3. The ragdoll seam (game/figure/ragdoll.ts) — contract, not a solver

  The old JS Verlet solver was deliberately dropped ("likely problematic the moment it takes a
  real load"). What survives:
  - The seam: bones-in/bones-out. A future host (Zig) solver only produces bone positions;
  buildRigFrameFromBones dresses them.
  - RAGDOLL_TUNING (a P2 data table): the 15-joint body graph, masses, stiffness, gravity,
  friction, iterations — every behavior number of the reference solver, kept as data the future
  host feature will consume.
  - ragdollHostReady() is honestly hardcoded false until the physics lane (__game_physics_*,
  V18) lands.
  
  The hard rule on top: render is preview-only; the game runs the bake

  This is V2-AMENDED and it's load-bearing:

  - render.tsx (FigureMeshes, buildPartRender, CharacterCaptures) renders a figure as live
  Scene3D.Mesh nodes — editor/lab preview ONLY. Per-figure-per-frame JS rig evaluation never
  ships in the compiled game. Live-sculpted figures take a dynamicKey (dyn slot); static figures
  (NPCs/rosters) pass intern so geometry lives in the big retained buffer — a crowd on dyn
  slots starves the pool and drops heads.
  - bake.ts → compile/playerModel.ts is the game path. At compile time it bakes the figure to
  host-shaped mesh groups and pre-samples animation clips into keyframes: idle (stand), an
  N-frame walk cycle, a jump (built from a DSL string [0.24, both_arms, lift_and_bend; 0.24, 
  both_legs, kick; 0.24, body, crouch] sampled through sampleAnimationTimeline), plus sit/lay
  via single actions. NPCs reuse the same PLAYER_ANIMATION because every figure with the same
  outfit bakes to the same node count.

  So: authoring evaluates bones live in React; the shipped game plays baked keyframe clips the
  host interpolates — no reconciler in the hot path.

  Consumers right now

  - Embodied.tsx / editors/play/PlayRoute.tsx — live player (buildRigFrame + FigureMeshes, gait
  phase fed from movement)
  - editors/workbench/characters/DressedStage.tsx + editors/characters/animPresets.ts —
  character editor with DSL-scripted animation playback
  - editors/workbench/vehicles/Stage.tsx + game/cutscene/ — vehicles and cutscenes both drive
  off GAME_ANIMATION (vehicles use the wheel/suspension aliases)
  - labs/combat-arena.tsx — combat figures, damage zones
  - compile/playerModel.ts / npcModels.ts — the compiled bake

  Net summary: a 25-bone hand-built FK skeleton whose Bones record is the universal currency for
  assembly/clothing/hitboxes/anchors; a separate V6 action-DSL layer (parse + sin-weighted
  sample, body+face+vehicle aliases) that modulates poses without touching the figure module; a
  ragdoll contract (seam + tuning table) waiting on a Zig host solver; and a strict split where
  live React mesh rendering is preview-only while the compiled game ships pre-baked keyframe
  clips. Studio (the editor for one part) needs to produce part-shaped output. Specifically: an EditMesh with named connection points that other parts can mount to. The connection points are part-of-the-data, not metadata added later.
A tire EditMesh has: the tire geometry + a mount point at the hub center, with an axis vector for the rotation, and a size constraint for the matching axle hole. The mount point is a typed connector. Other parts can mount to it if their connector matches.
A car body EditMesh has: the body geometry + 4 axle mount points + optional spoiler mount point + optional roof mount point. Each mount point is typed. Spoiler mounts to spoiler-mount; tire mounts to axle-mount; not interchangeable. The type prevents you from accidentally mounting a tire where a spoiler goes.
A character body has: torso geometry + neck mount (head goes here) + shoulder mounts × 2 (arms) + hip mounts × 2 (legs). The skeleton bones you already have basically are these mount points. The 25-bone skeleton encodes which parts attach where. But right now those connections are implicit in code — the rig builder knows that "head goes above torso at the neck position." The Lego refactor is to make those connections explicit data on the parts themselves.
This is exactly the move you did with the road system. Roads aren't painted cells; they're spines with plot points that connect via shared endpoints. Connection happens at named typed points. Parts are roads; mount points are plot points. Same architectural pattern, applied to mesh composition. Why this is the right shape for what you actually want to build:
You want to author 50 tires once, then any car can use any tire. You want to author 30 hands once, then any character can use any hand. You want to author 10 spoilers, 8 roofs, 15 hoods. The combinatorial explosion of unique vehicles comes from composition of parts, not from authoring whole vehicles.
Math: if you have 8 bodies × 15 tires × 10 spoilers × 8 hoods = 9,600 unique cars. From ~40 authored parts. Same approach as your building vocabulary, applied to vehicles. The vocabulary is small; the compositions are unbounded.
Characters work the same: 5 torsos × 6 heads × 8 hands × 8 feet × 4 height variants = 7,680 unique characters. From ~30 authored parts. And each character's customization (skin tone, clothing, scale) multiplies again.
You can't get this from authoring whole characters or whole vehicles. You'd burn out at 50 hand-authored characters. You can easily get it from authoring 30 parts and letting composition do the rest. The Lego model is what makes solo-dev content scale
resolution: Captured as the cornerstone (Part 0): the Lego composition model — author PARTS with typed MountPoints and mend them at matching connectors (a plug seats only in a same-typed socket), NOT one molded mesh. Bones are the mount graph made explicit; same pattern as the road grammar. Mount data landed and tested in editMesh.ts (MountPoint + mountsCompatible, 9/9). Corrected the earlier monolith drift in the doc. User-confirmed.
